newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Industrial stoppages seen in Western Australia.
newsitem.headline: Industrial stoppages seen in Western Australia.

text.p: Widespread industrial action is expected in Western Australia on Tuesday as the state's upper house of parliament examines a new industrial relations bill.
Union leaders said there would be work stoppages in various industrial sectors and a rally in Perth.
"It will not be a general stoppage but there will be action throughout the state," the Trades and Labor Council's Assistant Secretary, Stephanie Mayman said today.

"The final details won't be known until the 11th hour because meetings are going on today. But there are actions planned that will affect transport, power, ports, meat exports, mines, schools, the public service, hospitals and child care.
"Some workers are stopping for 24 hours, some for half a day and some just for the rally. We expect the rally to be bigger than anything we've ever done like it before."

The Labor Relations Legislation Amendment Bill was passed in the Legislative Assembly earlier this month and was expected to go to the Legislative Council, where the Government holds a one-seat majority, on Tuesday.

The bill provides for pre-strike secret ballots, limits union access to workplaces to issues affecting union members, denies union access to non-union members' wage records without employer permission, and requires unions to have majority membership support before making political donations.
The legislation has been criticised by church leaders as unnecessary and has prompted the ACTU to threaten a blockade to coincide with tomorrow's "Day of Action".

Mayman said the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), the top international trade union body, had also come out against the legislation and the ACTU had indicated it would lodge a complaint through the ICFTU with the International Labor Organisation in Geneva.

On Friday, state premier Richard Court met trades union leaders to hear their case against the legislation. The West Australian newsaper on Monday quoted Court as saying the government would make amendments but refusing to give details.
Industrial Relations Minister Graham Kierath, who returned to Perth on Sunday from a visit to China and Vietnam, said the visit had strenthened his resolve on the issue.

"There are 1.2 billion people in China producing very high quality products with wage rates one tenth of those in Australia so we have to be creative, innovative and more productive if we are going to compete," Kierath said.

"The government's "Productivity WA 2000 Vision and Plan" aims to achieve the highest standards of living in this State by the year 2000 but this cannot be achieved with labour laws written by past Labor Governments to suit their union power
Mayman said these comments were "a clear indication these laws are intended to make working Western Australians poorer."
"We will maintain our fight until this legislation is gone," Mayman said. "It is damning on working people and citizens with democratic rights."
